title: The Impact of Legal AI — A deeper dive into the RSGI/Harvey adoption report
author: Legal IT Insider

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The excerpt aligns with the cluster’s caution that AI benefits require better measurement, but it reports only the study’s scope and commissioning context, not substantive findings on bounded productivity, verification, competence risks or workflow reconfiguration. It therefore does not establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: While the benefits of AI are increasingly clear, the methods for measuring them are still maturing.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of Harvey as an increasingly adopted workflow tool that may strengthen in-house capacity, reduce spending on outside counsel and ALSPs, and prompt new service and business-model discussions. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution that reported benefits come from a small, advanced customer group and that value measurement remains immature.
qs: Corporate lawyers say that the tool has enabled their legal team to take on more work in-house and reduce their external counsel and also ALSP spend.
While the benefits of AI are increasingly clear, the methods for measuring them are still maturing.

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between usage and demonstrated value. It reports larger estimated time savings among power users and rapid benefits among established Harvey customers, while expressly cautioning that usage does not invariably produce savings, measurement methods remain immature, and the findings come from a predominantly experienced customer sample.
qs: A further valuable metric remains usage, with one CIO noting that while usage doesn’t always translate into time savings, there is a fairly strong correlation.
Time savings are mostly estimates, it was noted.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s qualified treatment of Harvey’s adoption evidence: it reports early business impact while acknowledging that the study mixes metrics with anecdotes, uses mostly established customers and relies on immature measurement methods. It does not independently establish—or directly assess—durable defensibility.
qs: While the benefits of AI are increasingly clear, the methods for measuring them are still maturing.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective, task-level deployment by reporting meaningful speed and time-saving benefits, especially in data-heavy extraction, while cautioning that most savings are estimated and that the in-house sample is unusually advanced. Its reported insourcing and client-delivery effects also align with work and provider-model redesign, without establishing general legal competence or market-wide outcomes.
qs: ***Practice areas/work type***   The greatest benefit is often gained in data-heavy extraction across practice areas and by individuals.

kp.k: Study covers established Harvey customers, with vendor commissioning disclosed
kp.d: Legal IT Insider reports on RSGI's November 2025 research surveying 40 organisations: 29 law firms and 11 in-house teams, geographically dispersed across Harvey's client base. Two thirds had used Harvey for over 12 months; organisations ranged from a 30-person in-house team to a 5,000-strong law firm. Many were early GenAI adopters, while in-house participants tended to be newer customers. Harvey commissioned the research on the stated basis of independent findings; the article discusses results with Harvey's head of customer engagement, K-Ming Lee.
qs: The 40 organisations polled in this evidence-based report were made up of 29 law firms and 11 in-house teams
Two thirds of participants had used Harvey for over 12 months and the teams surveyed ranged from a 30-person in-house team to 5,000-strong law firm.
the report, which was commissioned by Harvey on the basis that it would be entirely independent in its findings.

kp.k: Impact measurement combines quantitative metrics and anecdotal evidence
kp.d: The article emphasises that methods for measuring AI benefits remain immature. The study used both quantifiable metrics and anecdotal evidence, and most reported time savings were estimates. A participating CIO regarded usage as a useful indicator with a fairly strong correlation to time savings, while cautioning that usage does not always produce savings.
qs: While the benefits of AI are increasingly clear, the methods for measuring them are still maturing.
Impact was decided by quantifiable metrics but also anecdotal evidence
Time savings are mostly estimates, it was noted.
A further valuable metric remains usage, with one CIO noting that while usage doesn’t always translate into time savings, there is a fairly strong correlation.

kp.k: Respondents report benefits within months of purchasing Harvey
kp.d: Lee reports that two-thirds of responding customers experienced benefits within 90 days and nearly a third within 30 days. The article presents this as evidence of measurable impact within a quarter, rather than a finding about all legal-AI adopters. It also reports unanimous agreement among participating law firms that their lawyers would be upset or disappointed if Harvey were removed.
qs: predominantly two-thirds of our customers that responded say they had benefits within 90 days, and nearly a third of them said they had benefits within 30 days as well.
Interestingly, law firms were unanimous that their lawyers would be upset or disappointed if Harvey was taken away.

kp.k: Estimated time savings vary by user intensity and setting
kp.d: Some 72% of law firms and 90% of in-house participants supplied weekly time-saving estimates distinguishing power users from standard users; 85% of participants across both settings agreed work was executed faster using Harvey. The final reported monthly savings were 36.9 hours for law-firm power users and 15.7 for standard users, compared with 28.3 and 11.8 hours respectively in-house. These are reported estimates, not presented as directly measured productivity gains.
qs: Some 72% of law firms and 90% of in-house participants provided estimates of time savings per week, split between power users and standard users.
The majority (85%) of participants from law firms and in-house teams agreed that legal work is being executed faster using Harvey.

The final data from the report shows that law firm power users save 36.9 hours a month using Harvey and standard users save 15.7 hours. In-house that figure is 28.3 hours for power users and 11.8 for standard users.

kp.k: Data-heavy extraction features prominently among beneficial uses
kp.d: The article identifies data-heavy extraction as an especially beneficial application across practice areas. Transactions and litigation were the most frequently mentioned law-firm practice areas, with 25 and 22 participant mentions respectively, followed by IP and real estate, reported as mentioned by six participants.
qs: The greatest benefit is often gained in data-heavy extraction across practice areas and by individuals.

For law firms, the practice areas mentioned most frequently were transactions (mentioned by 25 participants) and litigation (by 22 participants), followed by IP and real estate (mentioned by six participants).

kp.k: AI fluency is associated with deeper use and value
kp.d: Lee interprets the report as showing that increased organisational fluency with AI brings more power users and deeper use, which he associates with incremental value. This is the vendor interviewee's account of the report, without a quantified relationship supplied in the article.
qs: The report does show that as a client becomes more fluent in using AI as a whole, the number of power users will go up, and the depth will go up in terms of how they are using it. That’s when they are really seeing incremental value.

kp.k: Harvey reportedly opens client conversations about business models
kp.d: Participating law firms strongly agreed that Harvey supports better client relationships. Lee characterises the mechanism as opening conversations about AI, different business models and different ways to deliver value. The article reports relationship benefits and new discussions, not demonstrated changes to pricing arrangements or firm structures.
qs: Law firms agreed strongly that Harvey enables them to build better relationships with clients.
It’s almost like Harvey has provided a gateway for them to start talking about a different business model, or start talking about AI, start talking about a different way to deliver value.

kp.k: In-house respondents report reduced external counsel and ALSP spending
kp.d: Corporate lawyers report that Harvey enables their teams to retain more work internally and reduce spending on external counsel and alternative legal service providers. The article highlights the implications for private-practice firms but qualifies the finding by noting that these in-house teams are comparatively large and technologically advanced; no spending-reduction amounts are supplied.
qs: Corporate lawyers say that the tool has enabled their legal team to take on more work in-house and reduce their external counsel and also ALSP spend.
These in-house teams are comparatively large and technologically ahead of the game but this is a hugely interesting finding.

kp.k: Customers signal greater outside-counsel pressure in 2026
kp.d: Lee relays in-house customers' intentions to put more pressure on outside counsel in 2026 and measure cost savings from their own AI usage. This is a reported forward-looking customer intention, distinct from the study's claims of already reduced external spending.
qs: We’re starting to hear a lot more from our in-house teams that ‘2026 is the year that we do want to start putting more pressure on our outside counsel and measuring how we’re saving costs in our own AI usage and consumption.’

kp.k: Lee presents 2025 as adoption beyond extended pilots
kp.d: One stated survey objective was to demonstrate that legal AI had moved beyond pilots amid continued intensive evaluation. Lee says pilots associated with 2024 extended into 2025, but interprets Harvey's customer experience as supporting predictions that 2025 would be the year of adoption. He explicitly limits this observation to the vendor's customer base.
qs: One of the key objectives of the survey was to prove that legal AI has moved well beyond the pilot phase

Everyone talked about 2024 being the year of pilots, which extended into 2025 as well. A lot of people predicted that 2025 would be the year of adoption and from our customer base, at least, that’s definitely what we’re seeing.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The article reports that Harvey delivers rapid measurable benefits and faster legal work, with greater time savings for power users.
pts.d: Reporting the RSGI/Harvey findings, the author says customers often see measurable impact within three months. Interviewee K-Ming Lee, Harvey’s head of customer engagement, states that approximately two-thirds of respondents reported benefits within 90 days and nearly one-third within 30 days. The article reports that 85% of participating law firms and in-house teams agreed that work was executed faster. Reported monthly time savings were 36.9 hours for law-firm power users versus 15.7 for standard users, and 28.3 versus 11.8 hours for in-house users. These savings are predominantly estimates, not presented as directly observed measurements. The author also reports unanimous agreement among participating law firms that their lawyers would be upset or disappointed if Harvey were removed.

pts.k: Greater AI fluency is associated with deeper use and incremental value; data-heavy extraction is identified as particularly beneficial.
pts.d: Lee interprets the report as showing that increasing client fluency in AI brings more power users, deeper use and incremental value. The author reports that data-heavy extraction often yields the greatest benefit across practice areas. Transactions and litigation were the practice areas mentioned most frequently by law-firm respondents, with 25 and 22 mentions respectively; IP and real estate followed, reported as mentioned by six participants. These are respondent mentions, rather than comparative performance benchmarks.

pts.k: Harvey is said to improve law-firm client relationships by opening conversations about AI, business models and delivery of value.
pts.d: The author reports strong agreement among participating law firms that Harvey supports better client relationships. Lee attributes this improvement to new conversations about business models and how firms deliver value. The claim concerns reported relationship benefits and opportunities for discussion; the article does not establish that firms have actually changed their pricing or business models.

pts.k: The article reports in-house work retention and reduced external-provider spending, while Lee describes customer intentions to increase pressure on outside counsel in 2026.
pts.d: The author reports corporate lawyers’ claims that Harvey allows their departments to handle more work internally and reduce spending on outside counsel and alternative legal service providers. No quantified spending reduction is supplied. The author qualifies these findings by noting that the surveyed in-house teams are comparatively large and technologically advanced. Lee reports hearing intentions from in-house customers to put more pressure on outside counsel and measure savings from their own AI use in 2026; this is a statement of customer intentions, not an established future market outcome.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is a Harvey-commissioned survey of 40 customer organisations, supplemented by qualitative testimony and Lee’s interpretation.
pts.d: The December 2, 2025 article draws on RSGI research published in November and an interview with Lee. The study surveyed 29 law firms and 11 in-house teams, geographically dispersed across Harvey’s client base and ranging from a 30-person in-house team to a 5,000-person firm. The article describes the report as commissioned by Harvey on the basis of independent findings. Many participants were early adopters, and two-thirds had used Harvey for more than 12 months. The author explicitly says impact was assessed using both quantifiable metrics and anecdotes because measurement frameworks are still developing. Time-saving estimates were provided by 72% of law-firm participants and 90% of in-house participants. The article offers neither model-performance benchmarks nor quantified external-spending results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern adoption and reported benefits through late 2025, principally among established customers; outside-counsel pressure is prospective for 2026.
pts.d: Lee says adoption, rather than just piloting, is visible in Harvey’s customer base in 2025, while acknowledging that pilots extended from 2024 into 2025. The author describes demonstrating movement beyond pilots as an objective of the survey. Benefits are reported within 30–90 days of purchase, but the sample largely consists of customers with at least a year of experience, some with 18 months; in-house customers tended to be newer. Incremental value is conditional on developing AI fluency and deeper use. The article does not present these findings as representative of all legal organisations, and Lee expressly limits his adoption observation to Harvey’s customer base.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The identified effects concern law-firm lawyers, corporate legal departments, their clients and external legal-service providers.
pts.d: Law-firm and in-house users reportedly gain time, with larger estimated gains for power users than standard users. Lawyers doing data-heavy extraction, particularly in transactions and litigation, are highlighted as beneficiaries. Firms reportedly gain improved client relationships and opportunities to discuss service delivery. Corporate legal departments reportedly gain capacity to retain work internally. Outside counsel and ALSPs are identified as providers whose spending allocations may fall and who may face greater client pressure in 2026. The source does not claim lawyer job losses, staffing-structure changes or improvements in public access to justice.
